newsitem.title: USA: AOL members may be surprised by next bills.
newsitem.headline: AOL members may be surprised by next bills.

text.p: Many America Online Inc members are rejoicing at the company's new flat-rate pricing plan of unlimted usage for $19.95 a month, but some subscribers are likely in for a shock when they get their next monthly bill.

Last week, America Online announced its much-expected unlimited pricing plan. But analysts said some members may be surprised because AOL plans to automatically convert all its seven million subscribers to the new flat rate pricing, unless a member requests to be put on a different billing plan.
"Our goal is to make sure we pro-actively communicate with all of our members," said an America Online spokeswoman.

"We have had an overwhelming response (to the new pricing plan)," the AOL spokeswoman said, adding that it was too early to tell how many subscribers the company expects will decide to stay at the $19.95 unlimited rate.

"In price testing of the $19.95 plan, it was very positive because it showed members preferred to pay one price," she said. AOL currently is informing its members of the new plan in several ways on the service, such as a message about the new pricing when a member signs on, with an area to read more.
But analysts warn that AOL risks losing some of its members through the default plan, which takes place next month.

"There will be a portion of the membership that will be less than happy and we will see what happens, whether they churn off," said Scott Reamer, a Cowen & Co analyst. "But in mass, I think there are quite a few people who will make a conscious decision not to go back (to the old pricing)."

Arlen Communications Inc in Bethesda, Md. estimates that AOL will lose approximately 200,000 members to the "light" rate plan of $4.95 a month for three hours. AOL also said that current members can be grandfathered to maintain their $9.95 a month for 10 hours if they choose. Members have three months to decide what kind of pricing plan they want, AOL said.

"For some people it will be a surprise and then it will be a hassle to make calls, but it's been the industry practice to just bill whatever the pricing is and the consumer has to be pro-active," said Adam Schoenfeld, a vice president at Jupiter Communications. "There is nothing sinister behind it."

AOL said that it is looking at other ways to let its subscribers know about its pricing plans. The pricing plan is now highlighted in chairman Steve Case's November letter to members, AOL's Welcome screen, the company's 800 number and the billing section of the service explains all the details.
